Why graph a system?

A system of linear equations asks for ordered pairs that satisfy both equations. On a coordinate plane, those pairs appear where the graphs meet. The intersection is a solution because it lies on both lines.
Read coordinates correctly
Read a plotted point as x comma y. First move horizontally to find x, then vertically to find y. A guessed crossing is not enough: always check the ordered pair in both original equations.
First worked intersection
Graph y equals x plus 1 and y equals negative x plus 5. Set the outputs equal: x plus 1 equals negative x plus 5. Then 2x equals 4, so x equals 2 and y equals 3.
Verify the first example
At x equals 2, the first line gives y equals 3. The second gives negative 2 plus 5 equals 3. Therefore 2 comma 3 is on both lines and is the exact solution.
Plot lines accurately
For y equals m x plus b, start at the y intercept b, then use slope m as rise over run. For each line, check three plotted points by substituting their x coordinates into the equation.
Second worked intersection
Graph y equals 2x minus 1 and y equals x plus 2. The graphs meet at 3 comma 5. Verify: 2 times 3 minus 1 equals 5, and 3 plus 2 equals 5.
When lines are parallel
Two distinct lines with equal slopes do not cross. For example, y equals 4x plus 1 and y equals 4x minus 6 have the same slope and different intercepts, so there is no solution.
When lines coincide

If the equations describe the same line, every point on that line is shared. For example, 2y equals 6x plus 4 simplifies to y equals 3x plus 2. With that same second equation, there are infinitely many solutions.
Fractional-slope example
Graph y equals one third x plus 2 and y equals negative two thirds x plus 5. Equate the outputs. One third x plus 2 equals negative two thirds x plus 5. Therefore x equals 3 and y equals 3.
Desmos strategy

Enter y equals 2x plus 1 and y equals negative x plus 7 on separate Desmos lines. Look for their intersection at 2 comma 5. Use the coordinate as the solution, then verify by substitution. Desmos is often faster for awkward graph scales; exact algebra can be faster for simple integers.
Avoid common mistakes

Do not confuse the x and y coordinates. Do not pick a point that lies on only one graph. Parallel lines have no intersection, while equivalent equations overlap everywhere. Verify exact coordinates rather than rounding a sketch.
